p.x:
Last Saturday, my older sister Ploy got married. Her husband, Tom, is from Australia. They first got to know each other at university in Bangkok five years ago. At first they were just friends, but then Tom asked her on a date, and she became his girlfriend. Tom says he was in love with her from the first day!
The wedding was in a beautiful garden in Chiang Mai. More than 200 guests came, including all our aunts, uncles and cousins. In the morning, there was a traditional Thai ceremony, and in the evening there was a big party. When the couple kissed, everyone cheered. My grandmother cried and gave everyone a hug.
Now Ploy and Tom are married, and they live in Melbourne. I really miss my sister, but we video chat every week. Tom's family is very kind to her. I'm happy that she's not single anymore and that she has found a husband who loves her.

p.t: How to Keep a Relationship Strong
p.x:
At the start of a relationship, everything feels exciting. Couples go on romantic dinners, send sweet messages and find each other incredibly attractive. But after a few years, especially once they are engaged or married, daily life can get in the way. So how do happy couples keep their relationship strong?
First, they communicate. Small problems can turn into a big argument if partners don't talk about them. Psychologists say that it's not arguing itself that causes couples to break up, but the way they argue. Respectful discussion is healthy; shouting and insults are not.
Second, happy couples make time for each other. Many celebrate their wedding anniversary with a trip, like a second honeymoon. Others simply have a "date night" every week. Third, they are loyal and supportive, especially during difficult times.
Even so, not every relationship lasts. In Thailand, the number of couples who divorce has risen over the past twenty years. My nephew, who works as a family counsellor, says the most common reason is that couples stop making an effort.

When Nok, a Thai engineer, met Lucas, a French architect, at a conference in Singapore, neither of them expected their relationship to last. For two years, they had a long-distance relationship, communicating through daily video calls and meeting only a few times a year. "It tested our commitment," Nok admits. "But it also taught us to express affection in words, not just actions."
When Lucas finally decided to propose, he flew to Bangkok without telling her and asked her family's permission first. The wedding combined both cultures: the bride wore a traditional Thai dress for the morning ceremony and a white gown in the evening, while the groom learned to perform a Thai blessing ritual.
Cross-cultural marriages bring their own challenges. Nok and Lucas have had to compromise on everything from food to holidays, and getting to know each other's in-laws was not always easy. "My mother-in-law and I didn't speak the same language at first," Nok laughs.
Nok's grandmother, a widow who had been married for fifty years, gave them simple advice: "Love isn't about finding your soulmate. It's about choosing the same person every day." Some friends warned Nok that she would end up heartbroken. Ten years later, the couple are still happily married.
